title: The Window · 1
paragraphs: “Yes, of course, if it’s fine tomorrow,” said Mrs. Ramsay. “But you’ll have to be up at the crack of dawn,” she added.

To her son these words brought an extraordinary joy. It was as if the trip were settled and bound to happen, as if the wonder he had looked forward to for years and years, it seemed, were now within reach, after just one night of darkness and one day’s sail. He belonged, even at the age of six, to that great clan who cannot keep one feeling separate from another, but must let their hopes for the future, with all its joys and sorrows, cloud what is actually in front of them. For people like this, even in earliest childhood, any turn of the wheel of sensation can crystallize and fix the moment on which its gloom or radiance falls. So James Ramsay, sitting on the floor cutting pictures out of the illustrated catalogue of the Army and Navy Stores, a London department store, gave the picture of a refrigerator a heavenly bliss as his mother spoke. It was fringed with joy. The wheelbarrow, the lawnmower, the sound of poplar trees, leaves whitening before rain, rooks cawing, brooms knocking, dresses rustling—all these were so colored and so distinct in his mind that he already had his own private code, his secret language. Yet he looked the very image of stark, uncompromising severity, with his high forehead and his fierce blue eyes, flawlessly candid and pure, frowning slightly at the sight of human weakness. So his mother, watching him steer his scissors neatly round the refrigerator, pictured him all in red and ermine as a judge on the Bench, or directing some stern and momentous undertaking in a crisis of public affairs.
“But,” said his father, stopping in front of the drawing-room window, “it won’t be fine.”

If there had been an axe within reach, or a poker, or any weapon that could have gashed a hole in his father’s chest and killed him, there and then, James would have grabbed it. Such were the extremes of feeling that Mr. Ramsay stirred in his children just by being there. He stood, as he stood now, lean as a knife, narrow as the blade of one, grinning sarcastically. He was pleased not only to disillusion his son and make fun of his wife, who was ten thousand times better than he was in every way (James thought), but also, secretly, to be vain about how accurate his judgment was. What he said was true. It was always true. He was incapable of untruth. He never tampered with a fact, never softened an unpleasant word to suit the pleasure or convenience of any living being, least of all his own children. They, born of his body, ought to know from childhood that life is difficult; that facts don’t bend; and that the passage to that fabled land where our brightest hopes are put out, where our frail boats go down in darkness (here Mr. Ramsay would straighten his back and narrow his little blue eyes at the horizon), is one that needs, above all, courage, truth, and the power to endure.

“But it may be fine—I expect it will be fine,” said Mrs. Ramsay, impatiently giving some little twist to the reddish-brown stocking she was knitting. If she got it done tonight, and if they went to the Lighthouse after all, it would be a present for the Lighthouse keeper’s little boy, whose hip was threatened with tuberculosis. It would go along with a heap of old magazines and some tobacco—really anything she could find lying around that nobody wanted and that only cluttered up the room. Those poor men must be bored to death, sitting all day with nothing to do except polish the lamp, trim the wick and rake about on their patch of garden; this would give them something to amuse them. Because how would you like being shut away for an entire month at a stretch, perhaps longer when the weather was stormy, on a rock no bigger than a tennis lawn? she would ask. With no letters, no newspapers, no one to see; if you had a wife, not seeing her, not knowing how your children were—whether they were sick, whether they had fallen and broken an arm or a leg; watching the same dreary waves break week after week, and then a dreadful storm rolling in, spray over the windows, birds flung against the lamp, the whole place shaking, and you unable to put your nose outside in case you were swept into the sea? How would you like that? she asked, turning especially to her daughters. And so, she went on, in a somewhat different tone, you must take them whatever comforts you can.

“It’s due west,” said Tansley the atheist, spreading his bony fingers so the wind blew between them; he was keeping Mr. Ramsay company on his evening walk, up and down, up and down the terrace. In other words, the wind was coming from exactly the worst direction for a landing at the Lighthouse. Yes, Mrs. Ramsay granted, he did say disagreeable things; it was nasty of him to press the point and make James more disappointed than ever. And yet she would not allow the children to laugh at him. “The atheist,” they called him; “the little atheist.” Rose made fun of him; so did Prue; so did Andrew, Jasper and Roger; even old Badger, who hadn’t a tooth left in his head, had bitten him, because he was (in Nancy’s words) the hundred-and-tenth young man to chase them all the way up to the Hebrides, when it was so much nicer to be left alone.

“Nonsense,” said Mrs. Ramsay, very sternly. Setting aside their habit of exaggerating, which they had inherited from her, and the suggestion (a true one) that she invited too many people to stay and had to lodge some of them in the town, she simply could not stand rudeness to her guests—especially to young men, who were poor as church mice, “exceptionally able,” according to her husband, great admirers of his, and who had come for a holiday. In fact the whole of the other sex was under her protection. Her reasons she could not have explained: their chivalry and bravery; the fact that they negotiated treaties, governed India, ran the world’s money; and lastly a certain attitude toward herself which no woman could fail to sense or to enjoy, something trusting, childlike, reverent, which an old woman might accept from a young man without any loss of dignity. And woe to the girl—please heaven it was none of her daughters!—who did not feel the value of it, and everything it implied, right down to the marrow of her bones.
She turned sternly on Nancy. He had not chased them, she said. He had been invited.

They must find some way out of it all. There might be a simpler way, a less exhausting way, she sighed. When she looked in the mirror and saw her gray hair and sunken cheek, at fifty, she thought that perhaps she could have handled things better—her husband; money; his books. But for her own part she would never for one second regret the choice she had made, run away from difficulties, or cut corners on her duties. She was a formidable sight just now. Only in silence, lifting their eyes from their plates after she had spoken so sharply about Charles Tansley, did her daughters—Prue, Nancy, Rose—dare to toy with the heretical ideas they had cooked up for themselves of a life unlike hers: in Paris, maybe; a wilder life; not forever looking after some man or other. For all of them silently questioned deference and chivalry, the Bank of England and the Indian Empire, ringed fingers and lace. And yet all of them also found in it something that was the very essence of beauty. It roused the manliness in their girlish hearts, and made them, sitting at the table under their mother’s gaze, respect her strange severity and her extreme courtesy—like a queen lifting a beggar’s dirty foot from the mud and washing it—when she reproached them so very sternly about that wretched atheist who had chased them to—or, strictly speaking, been asked to stay with them on—the Isle of Skye.

“There’ll be no landing at the Lighthouse tomorrow,” said Charles Tansley, clapping his hands together where he stood at the window with her husband. Surely he had said enough by now. She wished the two of them would go on with their talk and leave her and James in peace. She looked at him. The children said he was such a wretched specimen, all humps and hollows. He was no good at cricket; he poked about; he shuffled. A sarcastic brute, Andrew called him. They knew what he liked most: pacing endlessly up and down, up and down, beside Mr. Ramsay, discussing who had won this prize and who had won that, who was a “first-rate man” at Latin verse, who was “brilliant but I think fundamentally unsound,” who was beyond question the “ablest fellow in Balliol,” the Oxford college. Or who had hidden his light for the moment at Bristol or Bedford, but was sure to be heard of later, once his Prolegomena, his scholarly introduction, to some branch of mathematics or philosophy was published—Mr. Tansley happened to have the first pages in proof with him, if Mr. Ramsay cared to look at them. That was the kind of thing they talked about.

She couldn’t help laughing herself sometimes. The other day she had said something about “waves mountains high.” Yes, Charles Tansley agreed, it was a bit rough. “Aren’t you soaked right through?” she had asked. “Damp, not wet through,” Mr. Tansley replied, pinching his sleeve and feeling his socks.

But that wasn’t what bothered them, the children said. Not his face; not his manners. It was him—the way he saw things. Whenever they talked about something interesting—people, music, history, anything at all—or simply said what a fine evening it was, why not sit outside, their complaint about Charles Tansley was that he could never rest until he had twisted the whole subject round so that it somehow reflected on himself and made them look small. Somehow he set all their nerves on edge with that acid way he had of stripping the flesh and blood off everything. And he would go to art galleries, they said, and then ask you whether you liked his tie. God knows, said Rose, you didn’t.

The moment the meal was over, the eight sons and daughters of Mr. and Mrs. Ramsay slipped away from the dinner table as stealthily as deer and made for their bedrooms. These were their strongholds in a house where there was no other privacy, places to debate anything, everything: Tansley’s tie; the passing of the Reform Bill, the great voting reform of 1832; seabirds and butterflies; people. Meanwhile the sun poured into those attics, which were divided from each other by a single plank, so that every footstep could be clearly heard, and the Swiss girl sobbing for her father, who was dying of cancer in a valley of the Grisons, in Switzerland. The sun lit up bats, flannels, straw hats, inkpots, paint pots, beetles, and the skulls of small birds, and drew from the long frilled strips of seaweed pinned to the wall a smell of salt and weeds, which was in the towels too, gritty with sand from swimming.

Strife, divisions, differences of opinion, prejudices twisted into the very fiber of their being—oh, that they should start so early, Mrs. Ramsay lamented. They were so critical, her children. They talked such nonsense. She went out of the dining room, holding James by the hand, since he would not go with the others. It seemed such nonsense to her—inventing differences, when people, heaven knows, were different enough without that. The real differences, she thought, standing by the drawing-room window, are enough, quite enough. What she had in mind at that moment was rich and poor, high and low. The well-born received some respect from her, half grudging, for didn’t she have in her own veins the blood of that very noble, if slightly mythical, Italian house, whose daughters, scattered about English drawing rooms in the nineteenth century, had lisped so charmingly and stormed so wildly? All her wit and her bearing and her temper came from them, and not from the sluggish English or the cold Scots. But more deeply she brooded on the other problem, of rich and poor, and the things she saw with her own eyes, weekly, daily, here or in London. She would visit this widow or that struggling wife in person, with a bag on her arm and a notebook and pencil, and write down wages and spending, employment and unemployment, in columns carefully ruled for the purpose. She hoped that in this way she would stop being a private woman whose charity was half a sop to her own indignation, half a relief to her own curiosity, and would become what, with her untrained mind, she greatly admired: an investigator, shedding light on the social problem.

They were questions with no answer, it seemed to her, as she stood there holding James by the hand. That young man they all laughed at had followed her into the drawing room. He was standing by the table, fiddling awkwardly with something, feeling left out, as she could tell without turning round. Everyone had gone—the children; Minta Doyle and Paul Rayley; Augustus Carmichael; her husband—everyone had gone. So she turned with a sigh and said, “Would it bore you to come with me, Mr. Tansley?”

She had a dull errand in the town; she had a letter or two to write; she would be ten minutes perhaps; she would put on her hat. And there she was again, ten minutes later, with her basket and her parasol, giving off a sense of being ready, equipped for an outing. She had to interrupt it for a moment, though, as they passed the tennis lawn, to ask Mr. Carmichael if he wanted anything. He was basking there with his yellow cat’s eyes half open, so that, like a cat’s, they seemed to reflect the branches moving or the clouds passing, but gave no hint of any inner thoughts or feelings whatsoever.

For they were making the great expedition, she said, laughing. They were going to the town. “Stamps, writing paper, tobacco?” she suggested, stopping beside him. But no, he wanted nothing. His hands clasped themselves over his ample belly and his eyes blinked, as if he would have liked to answer her coaxing kindly (she was charming but a little nervous) but could not. He was sunk in a gray-green drowsiness that took them all in, without any need for words, in a vast and kindly lethargy of goodwill: the whole house; the whole world; all the people in it. For at lunch he had slipped a few drops of something into his glass, which explained, the children thought, the vivid streak of canary yellow in a mustache and beard that were otherwise milk-white. He wanted nothing, he murmured.

He ought to have been a great philosopher, Mrs. Ramsay said as they walked down the road toward the fishing village, but his marriage had been an unlucky one. Carrying her black parasol bolt upright, and moving with an air of expectation that was hard to describe, as though someone might be waiting for her just round the corner, she told him the story: a love affair at Oxford with some girl; marrying young; poverty; going out to India; translating a little poetry, “very beautifully, I believe”; being ready to teach the boys Persian or Hindustani, but honestly, what good was that?—and then ending up lying on the lawn, the way they had just seen him.

It flattered Tansley. After being snubbed, he found it soothing that Mrs. Ramsay should confide this to him. Charles Tansley perked up. She suggested, too, how great a man’s intellect was, even as it declined, and how every wife was subordinate to her husband’s work—not that she blamed the girl, and the marriage had been happy enough, she believed—and this made him more pleased with himself than he had been so far. He would have liked, say, if they had taken a cab, to be the one to pay. And her little bag—might he carry it? No, no, she said, she always carried _that_ herself. And she did, too. Yes, he could sense that about her. He sensed a great many things, one thing especially that excited and unsettled him for reasons he could not put into words. He wanted her to see him in academic cap and gown, walking in a procession. A fellowship, a professorship—he felt he could do anything, and pictured himself—but what was she looking at? A man pasting up a poster. The enormous flapping sheet smoothed itself flat, and every sweep of the brush uncovered more legs, hoops, horses, gleaming reds and blues, beautifully sleek, until half the wall was taken up by a circus advertisement: a hundred horsemen, twenty performing seals, lions, tigers. … Leaning forward, because she was shortsighted, she read aloud that it … “will visit this town.” What terribly dangerous work, she exclaimed, for a man with one arm to stand at the top of a ladder like that—he had lost his left arm in a reaping machine two years ago.
“Let’s all go!” she cried, walking on, as though all those horses and riders had filled her with a child’s delight and driven her pity from her mind.

“Let’s go,” he said, echoing her, but he clipped the words out so self-consciously that she winced. “Let us go to the Circus.” No. He couldn’t say it properly. He couldn’t feel it properly. But why not? she wondered. What was the matter with him? Just then she felt real warmth toward him. When they were children, she asked, hadn’t they been taken to circuses? Never, he replied, as though she had asked exactly the question he wanted to answer; as though for days he had been longing to tell her how they never went to circuses. It was a big family, nine brothers and sisters, and his father was a working man. “My father is a pharmacist, Mrs. Ramsay. He keeps a shop.” He had supported himself since the age of thirteen. Many winters he went without an overcoat. At college he could never “return hospitality” (those were his dry, stiff words). He had to make everything last twice as long as other people did; he smoked the cheapest tobacco, shag, the kind the old men smoked down on the docks. He worked hard—seven hours a day; his subject at present was the influence of something on somebody—they were walking along, and Mrs. Ramsay didn’t quite catch the sense, only a word here and there … dissertation … fellowship … readership … lectureship. The ugly academic jargon rattled off so smoothly that she could not keep up with it. But she told herself she understood now why the circus had knocked him off his perch, poor little man, and why he had burst out straight away with all that about his father and mother and his brothers and sisters; and she would see that nobody laughed at him any more; she would tell Prue. What he would have liked, she imagined, was to be able to say he had gone to an Ibsen play with the Ramsays. He was a terrible prig—oh yes, a bore past bearing. Because even though they had reached the town now, and were walking along the main street with carts grinding by over the cobbles, he kept on talking, about settlement houses, and teaching, and working men, and helping our own class, and lectures, until she gathered that his self-confidence was entirely restored, that he had got over the circus, and that he was about (and once more she felt warmly toward him) to tell her—but here the houses dropped away on either side, they came out onto the quay, and the whole bay lay open in front of them, and Mrs. Ramsay couldn’t help crying out, “Oh, how beautiful!” For the great plateful of blue water lay before her; the hoary Lighthouse, far off and austere, stood in the middle of it; and to the right, as far as she could see, the green sand dunes faded and fell away in soft low folds, with wild, streaming grasses on them, which always seemed to be running off into some moon country that no human being lived in.
That was the view, she said, stopping, her eyes turning grayer, that her husband loved.

She paused a moment. But now, she said, artists had come here. And there indeed, only a few steps away, stood one of them, in a Panama hat and yellow boots, gazing seriously, softly, absorbedly, though ten little boys were watching him, with a look of deep contentment on his round red face. He gazed, and then, when he had gazed, he dipped, steeping the tip of his brush in some soft mound of green or pink. Ever since Mr. Paunceforte had been there, three years before, all the pictures were like that, she said: green and gray, with lemon-colored sailboats, and pink women on the beach.

But her grandmother’s friends, she said, with a discreet glance as they went by, had gone to enormous trouble. They mixed their own colors to begin with, then ground them, and then covered them with damp cloths so they would stay moist.

So Mr. Tansley supposed she meant him to see that the man’s picture was skimpy—was that what you said? The colors weren’t solid? Was that what you said? Under the influence of that extraordinary emotion which had been growing all through the walk—it had begun in the garden when he wanted to carry her bag, and grown stronger in the town when he wanted to tell her everything about himself—he was coming to see himself, and everything he had ever known, gone slightly crooked. It was awfully strange.

There he stood in the front room of the cramped little house she had brought him to, waiting while she ran upstairs for a moment to see a woman. Above him he heard her quick step; heard her voice, bright, then quiet; looked at the mats, the tea caddies, the glass domes; waited with real impatience; looked eagerly ahead to the walk home, set on carrying her bag. Then he heard her come out; close a door; tell someone to keep the windows open and the doors shut, and to ask at the house for whatever they needed (she must be speaking to a child). And then, all of a sudden, in she came and stood silent for a moment (as though she had been playing a part up there, and now for a moment let herself simply be), stood perfectly still for a moment against a picture of Queen Victoria wearing the blue ribbon of the Garter; and all at once it came to him that it was this: it was this—she was the most beautiful person he had ever seen.

With stars in her eyes and veils in her hair, with cyclamen and wild violets—what was this nonsense he was thinking? She was fifty at least; she had eight children. Walking through fields of flowers and gathering to her breast broken buds and fallen lambs; with the stars in her eyes and the wind in her hair—He took her bag.

“Goodbye, Elsie,” she said, and they set off up the street, her parasol held upright, and she walking as though she expected to meet someone round the corner. And Charles Tansley, for the first time in his life, felt an extraordinary pride. A man who was digging in a drain stopped his digging and looked at her; let his arm hang down and looked at her. Charles Tansley felt an extraordinary pride; he felt the wind and the cyclamen and the violets, because for the first time in his life he was walking with a beautiful woman. He was holding her bag.
